title: Common earthing arrangements
summary: Explains why electrical systems are earthed and defines the TN-S, TN-C-S and TT earthing arrangements.

sections.heading: Reasons for earthing
paragraphs: There are three main reasons for earthing electrical systems. First, to maintain the potential of any part of the system at a defined value with respect to earth.

Second, to allow current to flow to earth in the event of a fault, so that the protective equipment will operate to isolate the faulty circuit. Third, to ensure that, in the event of a fault, apparatus normally 'dead' cannot reach a dangerous potential with respect to earth.
bullets: Maintain potential of any part of the system at a defined value with respect to earth
Allow fault current to flow to earth so protective equipment isolates the faulty circuit
Stop normally 'dead' apparatus reaching a dangerous potential with respect to earth in a fault

sections.heading: TN-S system
paragraphs: A TN-S system has separate neutral and protective conductors throughout the system.
bullets: TN-S: separate neutral and protective conductors throughout the system

sections.heading: TN-C-S system
paragraphs: A TN-C-S system is one in which neutral and protective functions are combined in a single (PEN) conductor in part of the system.
bullets: TN-C-S: neutral and protective functions combined in a single (PEN) conductor in part of the system

sections.heading: TT system
paragraphs: A TT system has one point of the source of energy directly earthed. The exposed-conductive-parts of the installation are connected to earth electrodes that are electrically independent of the earth electrodes of the source.
bullets: TT: one point of the source directly earthed
Exposed-conductive-parts connected to earth electrodes electrically independent of the source's electrodes

flashcards.front: Give the three main reasons for earthing electrical systems.
flashcards.back: To hold parts of the system at a defined potential with respect to earth; to let fault current flow so protection operates; to stop normally 'dead' apparatus reaching a dangerous potential.

flashcards.front: Why must current be able to flow to earth in a fault?
flashcards.back: So that the protective equipment will operate to isolate the faulty circuit.
A system having separate neutral and protective conductors throughout the system.
A system in which neutral and protective functions are combined in a single (PEN) conductor in part of the system.

flashcards.front: What does PEN stand for in a TN-C-S system, as used on the slides?
flashcards.back: It is the single conductor combining neutral and protective functions in part of the system.
A system with one point of the source directly earthed, the installation's exposed-conductive-parts connected to earth electrodes electrically independent of the source's electrodes.

flashcards.front: In a TT system, how are exposed-conductive-parts earthed?
flashcards.back: By earth electrodes electrically independent of the earth electrodes of the source.

flashcards.front: Which system has separate neutral and protective conductors throughout?
Which system combines neutral and protective functions in part of the system?

quiz.q: Which is one of the three main reasons for earthing electrical systems?
options: To maintain any part of the system at a defined potential with respect to earth
To increase the supply voltage
To reduce the cost of cables
To avoid the need for protective devices
quiz.why: Earthing maintains the potential of any part of the system at a defined value with respect to earth.

quiz.q: Why must fault current be able to flow to earth?
options: To charge the supply
So that the protective equipment will operate to isolate the faulty circuit
To raise the voltage of exposed metalwork
To stop current in the neutral
quiz.why: Current flowing to earth in a fault lets protective equipment operate and isolate the faulty circuit.

quiz.q: What is the aim regarding apparatus normally 'dead' in a fault?
options: It should carry the load current
It should become live to warn users
It cannot reach a dangerous potential with respect to earth
It should be disconnected from earth
quiz.why: Earthing ensures normally 'dead' apparatus cannot reach a dangerous potential with respect to earth in a fault.

quiz.q: Which earthing system has separate neutral and protective conductors throughout the system?
options: TT
TN-C-S
IT
TN-S
quiz.why: TN-S is a system having separate neutral and protective conductors throughout.

quiz.q: Which earthing system combines neutral and protective functions in a single (PEN) conductor in part of the system?
options: TN-C-S
TN-S
TT
TN-S-C
quiz.why: TN-C-S combines neutral and protective functions in a single PEN conductor in part of the system.

quiz.q: In a TT system, the exposed-conductive-parts are connected to what?
options: The neutral of the supply
Earth electrodes electrically independent of the source's electrodes
A PEN conductor
The cable sheath of the supply
quiz.why: In a TT system the exposed-conductive-parts connect to electrodes independent of those of the source.

quiz.q: Which system has one point of the source of energy directly earthed with independent installation electrodes?
options: TN-S
TN-C-S
TT
PEN
quiz.why: That is the definition of a TT system.

quiz.q: What does the 'PEN' conductor do in a TN-C-S system?
options: It acts only as a protective conductor
It acts only as a neutral
It connects the installation to an independent electrode
It combines neutral and protective functions
quiz.why: In TN-C-S the neutral and protective functions are combined in a single (PEN) conductor in part of the system.
